description: 60% hydration sourdough is firm, easy to shape, and kind to beginners. Work out the water, starter, and salt for any flour weight, with the table.

examples.result: Add 450 g flour, 250 g water, 100 g starter, and 10 g salt. Total dough 810 g.
steps: Starter is 20% of the flour: 500 × 0.20 = 100 g.
The starter is half flour and half water, so it brings 50 g of flour and 50 g of water.
Total water is 60% of the flour: 500 × 0.60 = 300 g. Water to add is 300 - 50 = 250 g.
Flour to add is 500 - 50 = 450 g. Salt is 2%: 500 × 0.02 = 10 g.

faqs.question: Is 60% hydration too low for sourdough?

felicityNote: My first sourdough was a 60% loaf, and I still bake at 60% when the week is busy. A dough that behaves is worth more than a dough that impresses.

parts.meaning: Total flour in the dough, always 100% in baker's percentages. The starter's flour is part of it.
Total water as a share of total flour. At 60%, every 100 g of flour holds 60 g of water.
Starter as a share of total flour. At 20%, 500 g of flour takes 100 g of starter.
A 100% hydration starter is half flour and half water, so half its weight is flour and half is water.
Salt as a share of total flour. At 2%, 500 g of flour takes 10 g of salt.

formula.text: Starter = flour × starter %. Flour to add = flour - starter ÷ 2. Water to add = flour × hydration % - starter ÷ 2. Salt = flour × salt %.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the flour and water
howToSteps.text: Put the bowl on the scale, zero it, and weigh in the flour to add, then the water to add. The calculator already subtracted the starter's flour and water, so weigh exactly what it says.

howToSteps.name: Add the starter and salt
howToSteps.text: Add the ripe starter, then the salt. Mix until no dry flour is left. The dough will feel firm and a little shaggy at first. That is normal at 60%.

howToSteps.name: Rest, then fold
howToSteps.text: Cover the bowl and rest for 30 minutes. Then give the dough a set of stretch and folds: lift one side up and over, turn the bowl, and repeat until you have folded all four sides.

howToSteps.name: Bulk ferment and shape
howToSteps.text: Let the dough rise until it is about half as big again, domed, and jiggly, then shape it into a round or a loaf. A firm dough shapes easily and holds its form in the basket.

lede: At 60% hydration the dough is firm, smooth, and easy to shape, which makes it the friendliest place to start with sourdough. Flour here means the total flour in the dough, including the flour inside the starter, so the hydration you ask for is the hydration you get.

name: 60% Hydration
summary: 500 g flour at 60% hydration: add 450 g flour, 250 g water, 100 g starter, 10 g salt.
title: Sourdough Calculator: 60% Hydration
tutorial: Sixty percent hydration is the firm end of sourdough. The dough holds its shape, barely sticks to your hands, and forgives a rough shaping job. If you have only ever made yeasted bread, this is the hydration that will feel familiar, and it is the one I would hand a first-time sourdough baker.

The numbers are simple because flour is always 100% in baker's percentages. For 500 g of total flour at 60% hydration, the dough holds 300 g of water in total. Your starter brings 50 g of that water with it, because 100 g of starter at 100% hydration is half flour and half water, so you add 250 g of water to the bowl. The starter also brings 50 g of flour, so you add 450 g of flour. Salt stays at 2%, which is 10 g.

Expect a tight crumb with small, even holes rather than the big open holes of a high-hydration loaf. That is a feature, not a failure. A tight crumb holds butter and jam, slices neatly for sandwiches, and toasts evenly. If your loaf is mostly destined for the toaster, 60% is a good place to stay.

A firm dough is also the easiest to read during bulk fermentation. It rises visibly, domes at the edges, and jiggles as one piece when you shake the bowl. Wetter doughs can look done when they are not, or keep spreading when you think they are ready. At 60% the signs are honest, which is why it is such a good teacher.

One caution: a firm dough dries out faster on the surface, so keep it covered during every rest. A damp tea towel or a shower cap over the bowl does the job. And if your flour is whole wheat or freshly milled, it will drink more water than white bread flour, so be ready to add a splash extra and treat 60% as a starting point, not a law.
